quote: Die $i^{\text{te}}$ Ueberschiebung einer Form mit ihrer Transformirten soll verschwinden. (Verallgemeinerung der Klein-Fuchsschen Formen mit Transformationen in sich wo $i = 1$ ist)
english: The i-th transvectant of a form with its transform should vanish. (Generalisation of the Klein–Fuchs forms with transformations into themselves, where i = 1.)
topic: A list of research ideas in invariant theory: groups of operations arising from irrational covariants, covariants defined by vanishing transvectants of binary forms of degree 7 and 10, a generalisation of Gordan's problem on sextic forms, vanishing transvectants of a form with its transform, re-proving a theorem of the dissertation by infinitesimal transformations, and a Lagrange problem on solving a binary form equal to a power of 2 in integers.

triage.modern_statement: Take a binary form f(x,y) of degree n and an invertible linear substitution S, with f^S = f∘S as the transformed form. The question is which pairs (f, S) make the i-th transvectant (f, f^S)_i vanish identically. When i = 1 the transvectant is the Jacobian of f and f^S. Two forms of the same degree have zero Jacobian exactly when they are proportional, so the i = 1 case gives f∘S = c·f. Those are the forms that admit linear transformations into themselves, which Klein (1875) and Fuchs studied in connection with finite groups of binary substitutions and algebraically integrable linear ODEs. Hilbert's note asks for the general version: for 1 < i ≤ n, describe and classify the forms whose i-th transvectant with some linear transform of themselves is zero. When i = n this means f is apolar to its own transform.
triage.answered_by: No one I could identify. The i = 1 case that Hilbert names as his starting point is classical: Klein, 'Ueber binäre Formen mit linearen Transformationen in sich selbst', Math. Ann. 9 (1875). Bolza's work on sextics (Amer. J. Math. 10, 1887) belongs to the same line. My searches turned up no work that takes up the generalisation to i > 1.

evidence.claim: The i = 1 case is the classical one: Klein, 'Ueber binäre Formen mit linearen Transformationen in sich selbst', Math. Annalen 9 (1875), pp. 183–208.

In 1875 Klein classified binary linear fractional transformations by looking geometrically at the binary forms they leave invariant. Jordan linked this to Fuchs's problem of the algebraic integration of linear ODEs.
Work on binary forms with linear transformations into themselves continued afterwards, e.g. O. Bolza, 'On Binary Sextics with Linear Transformations into Themselves', Amer. J. Math. 10 (1887).
Fuchs's work on algebraic solutions of linear ODEs used binary 'ground forms' tied to finite groups of linear substitutions. These are the 'Fuchs forms' in Hilbert's note.

Results that classify forms by vanishing transvectants do exist in other settings. For example, (f,f)_2 (the Hessian) vanishes exactly when f is a power of a linear form. None of the results I found involves a form paired with its own transform.

triage.why: The note is clear enough to state as a question, and the i = 1 case reduces correctly to Klein's 1875 forms with linear transformations into themselves, as Hilbert himself says. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. My few searches found no later paper that poses or solves the i > 1 version. Classical transvectant theory went out of fashion after Hilbert's finiteness theorems, which may be why. Because I searched only briefly and 19th-century invariant-theory literature is poorly indexed online, I can't rule out a forgotten treatment, perhaps a dissertation from the Klein or Gordan schools. So 'possibly_unexplored' carries low confidence, and I can't say whether anyone works on it today.
